en: How can I surrender my people
To the infidel son of the ogress?
If death has come, let me die;
Until my final hour arrives,
Let me try my strength in combat
With that dog, the ogress’s son.
While life still surges within me,
How can I surrender my homeland,
Its golden pillar and rallying cry?
Sarybai seems to have gone mad;
Until only one of my doomed people remains,
Let me test myself against him!
Grasping true steel and breaking his ranks,
If true death comes, let me fall to a bullet;
Let us take true aim at each other,
Hack one another down and die,
Let blood reveal the depth of our torment,
Let blood pour down in torrents.
Let courage show itself,
Let flowing blood spill like water
Against the infidel who seized the people.
His courage is cold, his venom strong;
If challenged, he lays a man flat.
If you grapple with the infidel,
Abandon all hope for your precious life!
He is skillful indeed, a hero indeed,
The very eye of a blood-drinker,
A black and terrible calamity,
Created as a dire scourge,
The very black disaster itself.
To devastate and tear up the land,
To drain blood without mercy,
Raging and standing proud,
This is the one who came prepared.
He is the black scourge itself,
Ready to mow down the ruined,
And all the settled people.
He skirted the edge of my hills;
I fought, but my strength did not suffice.
He laid low all who faced him,
And bound my heroes;
Not a single soul escaped
His fury without a wound.
Sarybai’s onslaught
Destroyed every living soul.
Short mace and broad shoulders—
Was Sarybai’s onslaught
Truly unmatched in all the world?
The earth cannot swallow all he grinds into it;
When the infidel rages,
The black earth with its grassy breast
Cannot endure this madman!
He will finish the battle at its appointed hour;
Sarybai the swine will consume
The abundant world and countless herds.
He will unleash a joyous slaughter,
Taking maidens and women as plunder—
The maddened swine will seize them!
He will tear down every house,
Fell the plane trees and lay them low,
And bring true disaster.
You made me a lion before all others,
Yet made me lesser than Sarybai;
You made me mightiest of all creation,
Then let a fairy maiden deceive me
And disgrace me before so many women.
Turning my words away from mankind,
Making my eyes unable to see,
Drying up my rivers and springs,
Stopping both my ears from hearing,
I was cast into an iron cage
And remained captive in the horde for many years.
Almighty, who fashioned all in the beginning,
You made me a son to the bloodthirsty lion,
Then made me the plunder and widow
Of Sarybai and Kök Monchok.
You let my living hands be bound,
When his turn came,
Rib bones and joints
Were torn layer by layer,
Spears and swords rang,
They strained and listened,
Let me pass through battle.
While my blessed people still stand,
If by chance I fall behind,
If fate leaves me grieving,
If I am struck down from behind,
And my cherished inherited people
Are seized by Sarybai,
My waist broken,
My nation laid waste,
What inheritance could I attain?
While my people remain unharmed,
For my great ancestral nation,
For the strength girded at my waist,
For the people who are my support,
For my precious inherited people,
Sarybai, who has challenged me,
I shall truly level my spear.
For my royal khan’s people,
I shall sacrifice this life.
Let my teeming people raise an outcry,
Saying, “Alas, our elder is dead,”
“He grappled fiercely with the dog
And gained his inheritance,”
“For the sake of the dear Kyrgyz people,
Our lionlike elder, tall as a mountain,
Before the people into whom he was born,
Departed as a sacrifice.”
“Counting his precious life no dearer than a fly,
Before his true people,
Our leopardlike elder passed away.”
Let the nation wail and the people weep,
Let the people’s hearts be torn,
Let their ribs seem rent apart,
Let the tears pour from their eyes.
Let the people lament and weep,
As though grief would crush them to dust.
He is not one to grow weary;
“Wretch, your sin will be upon you,”
He is not one to abandon us.
He seems savage, his venom strong,
He lays low everyone he meets;
In this wicked-looking infidel
Give up hope of any noble soul.
Would he ever cease his violence?
Amid the heavy calamity of his violence,
Would he spare a soul that begged?
Can we shrink away in fear?
Can this wondrous, Khizr-blessed people
Be handed over as tribute
To the infidel who oppresses us?
Would he spare a single soul?
Against the violent one who spares no life,
Against the black-hearted monster born,
Against the blood-spilling butcher,
Black-hearted and corrupt within,
Against this inescapable torment,
Why should I flinch
Before the black eyes of that brute?
Let us level our spears,
Fight without leaving one alive,
Make the whole world tremble,
Spend every resource of our minds,
Break every steadfast back,
Roam throughout the blessed Kyrgyz inheritance,
Leaving not a single soul untouched,
Against the infidel who has smeared the earth with blood,
Against the consummate, cunning warrior,
Who has brought the age to its end,
The warrior who has ruined the times,
I shall gird myself and wage war,
And meet him truly face-to-face.
Let ribs be split apart,
Let us shed blood without fleeing,
Let us wheel and grapple,
And stand facing one another.
When he fights, he is never sated with blood,
He who served as the Kyrgyz people’s shield
And pondered all their cares and sorrows.
When he met a foe, he charged,
And drank the blood of the enemy he encountered
As though it were kumis.
Whoever stirred his wrath,
He shed his blood and drove him away,
Driving his black-steel spear
Deep between his ribs.
He was the champion, he was the lion,
Throughout the whole wide world
He was the hero whose every deed prevailed.
His fame reached across the world;
When he girded his waist and roared,
The uproar reached even Beijing.
Will he lie down before Sarybai,
Saying, “He is a wrathful wrestler”?
Will he merely wander through the land,
Without clashing and battling,
Without meeting his foe and dying outright,
With blood spilled and sight extinguished,
Seeing no chance to turn back?
Will God strike down the bloodthirsty one?
Would he, because Sarybai is fierce,
Submit like a coward without courage,
Like a man struck by a curse,
And yield to his tyranny?
His forefather was a peerless warrior and lion.
Would he give the truly beloved Kyrgyz
As plunder into the hands
Of one vicious dog?
While the ill-fated man yet lives,
Would he submit to this conflict?
Would he give the fortified gates and beloved city,
The rightful Kyrgyz heirs,
Without first dying and perishing,
To that bloodthirsty Sarybai?
Let their worthy men be beaten,
And the dimple-mouthed, camel-eyed beauties—
Let this whole people grieve and weep,
Let the nation’s anguish be seen.
For my nation and my people,
Let this dear life be a sacrifice!
Let my bones remain upon the plain;
For my white-kalpak Kyrgyz people,
Let the magnanimous hero’s life be offered!
Our forefathers from whom we sprang
Were never defeated by a wrathful horde,
Never bowed their gaunt frames to a grasping foe.
Such was the people into whom we were born:
Not satisfied even when they drank by asking,
Never putting aside their hunger for more;
When driven through darkness,
They prowled like leopards,
No enemy raided their pastures,
None who opposed them remained alive;
Whenever diminished, they blazed anew,
Whenever destroyed, they grew stronger,
When calamity struck, they flared up,
They summered along the mountain slopes,
And none who grappled with them escaped unharmed.
From ancient times they feasted on fat,
Their cauldron was never without grease,
Their people clamored and ate meat;
How could I permit my valiant Kyrgyz nation
To be slaughtered?
For the people, for the nation,
Let me truly be the sacrifice!”
He couched his steel spear;
The bloodthirsty lion himself,
Burning with fury and grief,
Bound his precious life
To a single hair and cast it away.
When he came in violence,
Like one who would lay waste to hell itself,
What man could withstand
The magnanimous hero, lionlike in might?
He wore armor of blue steel
And charged alone against a host of foes,
Broad-flanked as a mountain ridge.
He made all who fought him submit,
Like the noble lion he was.
The layers of arrow-proof armor he wore
Numbered eighty-four,
And wherever he wheeled became fire.
When he raged like this,
He brought slaughter upon the world;
When he charged in fury,
He shattered the foe before him
And hurled them onto their backs.
When anger drove him into a frenzy,
If a formidable, tumultuous foe appeared,
None survived without being slain.
Such was this formidable lion;
When anyone provoked him,
When his enmity became true,
He would strike down even his own father—
Such was the imperious lion,
